# Review Global Fit Indices

## Null hypothesis in SEM 🤸

::: {.content-visible when-profile="teacher"}
::: {.notes}

H0: The model-implied covariance matrix equals the observed covariance matrix

H1: The model-implied covariance matrix does not equal the observed covariance matrix

Rejecting the null means the model we specified is not well-aligned to observed data (evidence AGAINST our hypothesis)
:::
:::

## Model Fit Indices Review


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="12%"}
**Index**

- χ²
- CFI
- RMSEA
- SRMR
- AIC
- BIC
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .smaller}
**Concept**

- A. Ave size of the differences btw observed and model-predicted correlations
- B. Error per df, adjusting for model complexity
- C. Fit penalized for complexity; penalty grows with sample size
- D. Is the model-implied covariance matrix different from observed?
- E. How much better the model is than a baseline model where nothing is related
- F. Fit penalized for complexity; fixed penalty per parameter
:::

::: {.column width="40%" .smaller}
**Thresholds**

1. ≥ .95 good; ≥ .90 acceptable
2. < competing model
3. ≤ .05 good; .05–.08 acceptable; ≥ .10 poor
4. Non-significant p supports hypothesis
5. ≤ .08 good
6. < competing model
:::

:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="teacher"}

## Activity: Answer key

```{=html}
<style>
.answer-key td:nth-child(n+2) { font-size: 0.7em; }
</style>
```

::: {.answer-key}

| Index | Concept | Threshold |
|------------|------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| χ² | D. Is the model-implied covariance matrix different from the observed one? | 4. Non-significant p supports the hypothesis |
| CFI | E. How much better the model is than a baseline model where nothing is related | 1. ≥ .95 good; ≥ .90 acceptable |
| RMSEA | B. Error per degree of freedom, adjusting for model complexity | 3. ≤ .05 good; .05–.08 acceptable; ≥ .10 poor |
| SRMR | A. Average size of the differences between observed and model-predicted correlations | 5. ≤ .08 good |
| AIC | F. Fit penalized for complexity; fixed penalty per parameter | 2 or 6. Lower than a competing model (no absolute cutoff) |
| BIC | C. Fit penalized for complexity; the penalty grows with sample size | 2 or 6. Lower than a competing model (no absolute cutoff) |

:::
:::


# Global Fit: Why we need many 

We'll compare some different scenarios to dig into what each tells us.

## Chi2: Same matrix, different N

Look at the lavaan model & draw the path diagram. 

```{r}
#| label: ex1-setup
#| echo: true
library(lavaan)

S <- lav_getcov(c(
  1.000,
  0.560, 1.000,
  0.600, 0.525, 1.000,
  0.256, 0.224, 0.300, 1.000,
  0.240, 0.210, 0.225, 0.600, 1.000,
  0.224, 0.196, 0.210, 0.560, 0.525, 1.000),
  names = paste0("x", 1:6))

ex1_model <- '
  F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  F2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
'

fit_small <- cfa(ex1_model, sample.cov = S, sample.nobs = 100)
fit_large <- cfa(ex1_model, sample.cov = S, sample.nobs = 5000)
```



## X2: Fit at N = 100 vs. N = 5,000

```{r}
#| label: ex1-table
fm <- function(fit) fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue"))
m1 <- fm(fit_small); m2 <- fm(fit_large)
crit <- qchisq(.95, df = m1["df"])
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", formatC(p, digits = 3, format = "f"))
sig <- function(p) ifelse(p < .05, "reject the null - hypothesis not supported", "fail to reject - hypothesis supported")

tab <- data.frame(
  Index = c("χ²", "df", "Critical χ² (α = .05)", "p-value", "Significant?"),
  `N = 100` = c(sprintf("%.3f", m1["chisq"]), m1["df"], sprintf("%.3f", crit),
                fmt_p(m1["pvalue"]), sig(m1["pvalue"])),
  `N = 5,000` = c(sprintf("%.3f", m2["chisq"]), m2["df"], sprintf("%.3f", crit),
                  fmt_p(m2["pvalue"]), sig(m2["pvalue"])),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr")
```


## X2: Takeaway

- Same relationships among the variables (same var/cov matrix), same model.
  - actual fit doesn't change. Only N
- χ² flipped from "supported" to "not supported"
- χ² is very sensitive to N, so can't tell us whether the model is a good one. 

## CFI: Grading on a curve

CFI asks: how much of the misfit in a baseline model does our model remove?

- χ² between baseline model & observed: χ²<sub>B</sub> 
  - Baseline: all variables assumed uncorrelated. High misfit
- χ² between theoretical model & observed: χ²<sub>M</sub>
  - In theory, smaller misfit

(CFI × 100) = % of the baseline misfit removed by theoretical model.

## Example 1: CFI at N = 100 vs. N = 5,000

```{r}
#| label: ex1-cfi
bm <- c("chisq", "df", "baseline.chisq", "baseline.df", "cfi")
cfi_tab <- data.frame(
  Index = c("Baseline χ²", "Baseline df", "Model χ²", "Model df", "CFI"),
  `N = 100`   = fitMeasures(fit_small, bm)[c(3, 4, 1, 2, 5)],
  `N = 5,000` = fitMeasures(fit_large, bm)[c(3, 4, 1, 2, 5)],
  check.names = FALSE
)
cfi_tab[, 2:3] <- lapply(cfi_tab[, 2:3], function(x) formatC(x, digits = 3, format = "f"))
cfi_tab[c(2, 4), 2:3] <- c("15", "15", "8", "8")
knitr::kable(cfi_tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr")
```

- Same verdict at n = 100 & n = 5000
  - addresses χ² problem

## CFI Shortcomings

What if the baseline changes? 

## CFI Shortcomings 2

How can the baseline change? Variables are more strongly correlated.

```{r}
#| label: cmp-setup
S_strong <- lav_getcov(c(
  1.000,
  0.765, 1.000,
  0.792, 0.748, 1.000,
  0.486, 0.459, 0.535, 1.000,
  0.475, 0.449, 0.465, 0.792, 1.000,
  0.459, 0.434, 0.449, 0.765, 0.748, 1.000),
  names = paste0("x", 1:6))

fit_orig   <- cfa(ex1_model, sample.cov = S,        sample.nobs = 1000)
fit_strong <- cfa(ex1_model, sample.cov = S_strong, sample.nobs = 1000)

cm <- c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "baseline.chisq", "cfi", "rmsea")
a <- fitMeasures(fit_orig, cm); b <- fitMeasures(fit_strong, cm)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 3, format = "f")
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 1, format = "f")
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 2, format = "f")
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", f3(p))
```

```{r}
#| label: cmp-cfi-table
cfi_cmp <- data.frame(
  Index = c("Range of correlations", "Baseline χ² (max misfit)", "Model χ² (df = 8)", "CFI"),
  Original = c(paste(f2(min(S[lower.tri(S)])), "–", f2(max(S[lower.tri(S)]))),
               f1(a["baseline.chisq"]), f1(a["chisq"]), f3(a["cfi"])),
  Strong   = c(paste(f2(min(S_strong[lower.tri(S_strong)])), "–", f2(max(S_strong[lower.tri(S_strong)]))),
               f1(b["baseline.chisq"]), f1(b["chisq"]), f3(b["cfi"]))
)
knitr::kable(cfi_cmp, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr")
```

- If we only look at CFI, it looks like the model performs well on both original and strong correlations. 
- Reality: there's just a ton more misfit in the strong model. 

## CFI Takeaway

- Baseline assumes no correlation between variables 
- If variables are actually correlated, misfit is inflated
- Large baseline misfit means even a very mediocre model can look good

Is CFI merely an effect of a large baseline mismatch? 

## RMSEA 

## RMSEA: Ave misfit / DF

Can it distinguish between the original & strongly correlated models?


## Original vs. strong: χ², CFI, and RMSEA

```{r}
#| label: cmp-all-table
all_cmp <- data.frame(
  Index = c("Baseline χ²", "Model χ²", "CFI", "RMSEA"),
  Original = c(f1(a["baseline.chisq"]), f1(a["chisq"]), f3(a["cfi"]), f3(a["rmsea"])),
  Strong   = c(f1(b["baseline.chisq"]), f1(b["chisq"]), f3(b["cfi"]), f3(b["rmsea"]))
)
knitr::kable(all_cmp, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr")
```

- RMSEA goes from good to acceptable, indicating worse fit

::: {.content-visible when-profile="teacher"}
::: {.notes}
Next up: SRMR, the average residual in correlation units. It is about .012 vs. .011 here, since the leftover misfit (the x3-x4 residual) is the same in both matrices.
:::
:::

## RMSEA 

RMSEA (Root Mean Square Error of Approximation)

- Does **not** use a baseline model, so it can't be propped up by a large baseline misfit.
- Based on the model's own misfit per degree of freedom: how far off is the model, adjusting for how simple or complex it is.
- Divides by N, which removes the sample-size inflation we saw with χ².

$$RMSEA = \sqrt{\frac{\max(\chi^2_M - df_M,\ 0)}{df_M\,(N - 1)}}$$

- Lower is better: ≤ .05 good; .05–.08 acceptable; ≥ .10 poor

## SRMR

## SRMR: a residual you can read

SRMR (Standardized Root Mean Square Residual)

- The typical size of the differences between observed and model-implied **correlations**.
- In correlation units: SRMR = .05 means "our model's correlations are off by about .05, typically."
- Compare RMSEA, which is χ²-based and has no direct units.
- Lower is better; ≤ .08 indicates good fit.

Caveats:

- No penalty for model complexity.
- Like RMSEA, can be shaky with small N or low loadings.
- A typical size can hide one large residual.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="teacher"}
::: {.notes}
SRMR is a root-mean-square, so "typical size" is a safer phrase than "average". The loading-size caveat is general and literature-based; our demo does not show SRMR moving with loadings (.012 vs. .011), unlike RMSEA (.019 vs. .061).
:::
:::

## Original vs. strong: RMSEA and SRMR

```{r}
#| label: cmp-srmr-table
cs <- c("rmsea", "srmr")
a2 <- fitMeasures(fit_orig, cs); b2 <- fitMeasures(fit_strong, cs)
srmr_cmp <- data.frame(
  Index = c("RMSEA", "SRMR"),
  Original = c(f3(a2["rmsea"]), f3(a2["srmr"])),
  Strong   = c(f3(b2["rmsea"]), f3(b2["srmr"])),
  `How to read it` = c("χ²-based misfit per df; no direct units",
                       "Typical residual correlation: off by about .01"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(srmr_cmp, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrl")
```

- SRMR is easy to say out loud: the model-implied correlations are off by about .01 in **both** cases, well under the .08 cutoff.
- RMSEA flags the strong matrix as worse, but the number itself is harder to interpret.
- Both are useful: RMSEA is a χ²-based absolute check, SRMR tells us how big the differences actually are.

## SRMR: where is the misfit?

Residual correlations (observed − model-implied) for the original data:

```{r}
#| label: srmr-resid
res <- as.matrix(lavResiduals(fit_orig, type = "cor")$cov)
res_fmt <- matrix(formatC(res, digits = 3, format = "f"), nrow(res),
                  dimnames = dimnames(res))
res_fmt[upper.tri(res_fmt, diag = TRUE)] <- ""
big <- lower.tri(res) & abs(res) >= .03
res_fmt[big] <- paste0("**", res_fmt[big], "**")
knitr::kable(res_fmt, align = "r")
```

- Almost every residual is near 0.
- The x3–x4 residual (.047) stands out. That is the misfit we built into the data: a relationship between x3 and x4 that our model ignores.
- SRMR summarizes these residuals in one number; the matrix shows **where** the model misses.

What are the shortcomings of each (why do we need so many)?

# Identification

How are the following related in CFA?

Specification, path diagram, information, information, parameters (lambda, psi, theta matrices), degrees of freedom, model implied covariance, observed covariance, model fit
